q: Should I rewind a burnt motor or replace it, and what does rewinding do to efficiency and CO2?
title: Rewind or replace a burnt motor?
short: Rewind when the motor is large, special or runs few hours, and the repair shop follows good practice. Replace with an IE3 or IE4 motor when it runs long hours, is a common size, or has been rewound before. A careless rewind can cost efficiency; a good one keeps it close to the original.

p: A study by EASA and AEMT on the effect of repair and rewinding on motor efficiency found that motors rewound with good practice kept their efficiency close to the original, while poor practice, such as stripping old windings by burning at uncontrolled high temperatures or changing the winding design, raised losses. IEC 60034-23:2019 sets out good repair practice. Ask your repair shop how it strips cores and whether it copies the original winding data.

sections.h: A decision rule at the moment of failure
ul: Replace: long running hours, a standard frame size available off the shelf, an old IE1 or unrated motor, or a motor already rewound once or twice.
Rewind: a large or special motor with long lead time, low running hours, or a newer high-efficiency motor with an undamaged core.
Either way: check why it failed, such as overload, single phasing, bearing failure or water ingress, so the next motor does not fail the same way.

sections.h: The formula for the extra energy
p: Extra kWh a year = output kW x running hours x (1 / efficiency after rewind minus 1 / efficiency of the new motor). Output kW is the motor's rated kW times its load factor. Multiply the extra kWh by 0.710 kg CO2 per kWh for Scope 2, and by your tariff for cost.

A good repair shop can give no-load current and loss readings before and after the rewind. Keep them with the job card. Compare the motor's running current at the same load before failure and after repair; a clear rise points to higher losses.

example.title: Illustrative example: a 30 kW motor at 75% load
lines: Output: 30 x 0.75 = 22.5 kW, for 6,000 hours a year
New IE3 motor: 93.6% (nominal for a 4-pole 30 kW motor; read yours from the nameplate)
Rewound motor: 92.1% (assumed 1.5 points lower after a poor rewind)
Extra energy: 0.3915 x 6,000 = 2,349 kWh a year
Extra CO2: 2,349 x 0.710 = 1,668 kg, about 1.7 t a year
example.note: The 1.5 point loss is an illustrative assumption, not a default; a good rewind may lose little or nothing.

senseible: Senseible converts kWh to CO2 at the CEA factor of 0.710 kg CO2 per kWh, so a more efficient motor shows up as lower Scope 2 in the records it builds from your electricity bills.
